newsitem.title: GERMANY: Wall Street woes knock 2.6 pct off Germany's DAX.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street woes knock 2.6 pct off Germany's DAX.

text.p: Blue chip German shares ended an edgy floor trading session with sharp losses on Thursday after fresh declines on Wall Street triggered more panic and investors braced themselves for what the afternoon would bring.
"It's just nerves, nerves and more nerves here," said a Frankfurt trader. "There is no hope of us decoupling from the U.S."
The 30-share DAX ended the session down 86.67 points, or 2.6 percent, at 3,215.24 points, finally holding above a key technical support level at 3,200 which it fell below in early trade.
But the extent of the decline on Thursday was deceptive as the market had already priced in much of Wall Street's weakness in late electronic trade on Wednesday.
The IBIS DAX index, which reflects all-day trade in DAX shares, was up around five points from its 3,210.94 close.

While most blue chips were under pressure, chemical firm BASF AG was firmer than average, ending down 15 pfennigs at 61.50 while AMB Holding, profiting from takeover speculation in the insurance sector, rose six percent to 730 marks.

"I think at this stage the market has even priced in very weak labour numbers from the U.S. on Friday," said Michael Vieker, manager of a 600-million-mark German equity fund for Muenchener Kapitalanlage AG in Munich.
The Friday jobs data, due at 1330 GMT, is expected to give the U.S. market its next clear direction, shedding more light on whether fears of more interest rate hikes are realistic.
Dow Jones Industrials fell 94 points to 6,517 points on Wednesday, keeping German attention riveted on the U.S.
Dealers said that while there was little fundamental reason for German shares to track the U.S., the psychological impact of Wall Street's decline was immense.
"It's clear we are at a different stage here in the economic cycle -- no-one is talking about a German rate hike today. But it still all depends on Wall Street," a dealer said.
The market paid minimal attention to domestic news, shrugging off a report showing faster than expected 1.9 percent growth in industrial output in February.

The Bundesbank's widely expected inaction on interest rates at its policy-setting meeting had no impact, nor did an announcement by Chancellor Helmut Kohl that he wanted to run for election again next year.
